I'm a Computer Science major, and I'm in my fourth year. My schedule this semester is really packed, but it's exciting to be taking higher-level courses. It feels surreal to be at this stage, looking back on how far I've come from my intro classes. Now I'm diving into complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even quantum computing basics. It's amazing how quickly time has passed!
store.1: I'm a Computer Science major, and I'm in my fourth year. My schedule this semester is really packed, but it's exciting to be taking higher-level courses. It feels surreal to be at this stage, looking back on how far I've come from my intro classes. Now I'm diving into complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even quantum computing basics. It's amazing how quickly time has passed!
store.2: My favorite class this semester is definitely Advanced Algorithms. I'm fascinated by theory that directly connects to real-world problem-solving, such as optimizing pathfinding in large networks or finding the fastest way to handle huge datasets with minimal time complexity. We've been exploring dynamic programming approaches and approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems. It's mind-bending, but in a good, challenging way. Our professor is great at explaining these complex concepts in an intuitive manner. She'll present a seemingly impossible problem and then show us a strategy to approximate a solution. Every time I leave that class, my brain is buzzing.
store.3: I'm also taking a Distributed Systems course(CS 2631), which is probably the second hardest. It's a lot of reading, group discussions, and we're working on a major project that simulates a decentralized file storage system. The group project is an adventure, as we have to collaborate with folks who have different coding styles and ideas about the final product. However, that's also the beauty of it. In a real-world setting, you're never working in a vacuum. You have to integrate your code with others' and handle issues like concurrency and node failures. It's nerve-wracking at times, like when I spent hours troubleshooting a weird bug that turned out to be a misplaced bracket in a config file. But once we fixed it and everything ran smoothly, it was a huge sense of accomplishment.
store.4: I'm also taking an elective in Game Design, which counts toward my major if I combine it with other classes. As a gamer at heart, this was a must-take. The professor is from the industry and worked on indie games that got some traction. We're learning about basic 2D and 3D engines, implementing physics, and even user experience design. It's incredibly fun because every assignment is super creative. Last time, I had to design a mini-game based on a labyrinth concept, focusing on balancing the difficulty curve to avoid frustrating players. Getting that design right was challenging, but it was rewarding to see it come together.
store.5: I'm also taking an Introduction to Quantum Computing class, which initially intimidated me. However, the professor's approach focuses on conceptual understanding rather than pure math. We're using code examples in frameworks that simulate quantum circuits, which makes it more accessible. We're modeling basic algorithms like Grover's and Shor's to see how they outperform classical methods. It's mind-blowing to see how quantum computing can solve problems more efficiently. This class has made me rethink how I approach problems and has opened up new perspectives.
store.6: I'm also taking a Capstone Project course, which is the sink-or-swim part of senior year. We have the entire semester to conceptualize, design, and build a software solution that solves a real problem. My group decided to work on a project that uses machine learning to analyze social media sentiment for better emergency response. It involves reading a firehose of tweets or posts and analyzing them for words that might suggest a disaster or crisis. We're building an interface that city officials or campus security could use to see real-time alerts. This project is pulling together everything I've learned as a CS major: database management, building an API, front-end interface, and the ML pipeline. We're also learning about project management and how to keep ourselves organized. One person on our team is the designated "Scrum Master," so each week we have sprints, daily stand-ups, and all that agile jazz. It's a lot, but if we can pull it off, I'll be super proud.
store.7: I'm also taking a Philosophy of Mind course as a humanities elective. It's my last required non-CS elective, and I chose it because it ties back into AI in interesting ways. We discuss consciousness, the concept of mind, and how it applies to artificial intelligence. The class is smaller, so we have a lot of discussions, which is a welcome change from coding in other classes. It's great to analyze abstract ideas and see the bigger picture, like the ethical implications of building AI systems that could mimic or simulate human thinking. I wrote a paper on whether strong AI could truly experience qualia, like the subjective experience of color or pain. It's a huge topic in the philosophy world, and researching it was fascinating. I believe bridging technical knowledge with ethical considerations is crucial, so I'm grateful for this perspective.
store.8: My schedule is quite packed, as you can imagine. Mondays and Wednesdays are the most hectic days. I start with Advanced Algorithms at 9:30 am, followed by a short break before my Distributed Systems lecture at 11:00 am. After lunch, I have the Capstone meeting, which can be a mix of lectures, lab work, and project team time. Tuesdays and Thursdays are a bit lighter with Quantum Computing in the morning and Game Design in the afternoon. Philosophy of Mind is on Thursday evenings, which can be tough if I'm tired from the rest of the day. Fridays are open, but I usually end up working on assignments, group projects, or labs. I also do some undergrad research hours in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific data sets. It's fascinating, but it definitely adds to the workload.
store.9: The biggest challenge this semester is balancing the group projects. Capstone alone can consume around ten hours a week, and if we encounter a major bug or if the model isn't training properly, it can be even more time-consuming. Additionally, the Distributed Systems project is another significant time commitment. My group meets at least twice a week to work on these projects. We also rely on Slack or Discord to stay updated and communicate effectively. Coordinating five different people's schedules can be a logistical nightmare, but it's also exciting. This is one of my last chances to fully invest in purely academic projects without the pressures of a job environment. It's a great opportunity to learn and grow.
store.10: I'm having a blast this semester. I used to dread the tougher CS classes because I was worried I wouldn't keep up, but now I've gotten better at problem-solving and time management. I still pull the occasional late night, but it's not as scary as it once was. Being a senior has given me a sense of confidence; I know that if I grind and keep my eye on the end goal, I'll eventually figure things out. The biggest takeaway is that after four years, you learn how to be resourceful, collaborate, and think critically. These classes are tough, no doubt, but they're also super rewarding. Everything I'm doing now feels like it's directly building toward my future career, and that's a great feeling.
store.11: I'm a fourth-year computer science major, and I have to say, my hobbies are what keep me sane. They help me come back to programming with a fresh perspective. It's important to take breaks and not be stuck behind my laptop 24/7.
store.12: Sailing is a hobby that brings me a sense of freedom and challenge. It's a great way to clear my mind and enjoy the outdoors. I feel lucky to have grown up near a marina and had the opportunity to learn how to sail. Now, whenever I can, I try to keep up with it by renting a boat through a local sailing club. It's a wonderful feeling to be out on the water, navigating through choppy seas and unpredictable winds. It's like solving a puzzle on a grand scale, which I find really appealing. I'm grateful for the break it gives me from the stresses of college life.
store.13: I started going to the gym regularly in college as a way to offset the sedentary lifestyle of being a computer science major. I began with a basic lifting routine and gradually increased my frequency and intensity over time. I love seeing incremental improvements in my strength and energy levels. Working out is not only a great stress-reliever but also enhances my mental clarity and productivity. It's a win-win for both my physical and mental health.
store.14: Gaming is a hobby that complements my interest in technology. I enjoy both PC and console games, but PC gaming is more convenient for me as a CS major. Lately, I've been fascinated by co-op survival games, which offer a unique blend of problem-solving and relaxation. I also occasionally indulge in fast-paced shooters, which provide a social and mental challenge. Gaming allows me to stay connected with friends and enjoy a different kind of strategic thinking. Additionally, I've experimented with game development using Unity and Unreal Engine, and I hope to explore this further in the future. It's exciting to bridge the gap between playing games and creating them.
store.15: Reading has been a lifelong passion for me, thanks to my mom's love for literature. She introduced me to fantasy and sci-fi novels when I was a kid, and I'd get lost in other worlds for hours. Even with a busy schedule, I try to squeeze in some reading before bed or on weekends. Lately, I've been fascinated by sci-fi novels that explore artificial intelligence. It's interesting to imagine future technology and how it might blur the lines between humans and machines. My current favorite AI-themed sci-fi book is 'The Infinity Courts' by Akemi Dawn Bowman. Reading books like this helps me consider the ethical and social implications of my academic interests, making it both a source of relaxation and a way to explore deeper questions about my future career.
store.16: I've found that scheduling my hobbies helps me maintain a healthy balance. I plan my week ahead and check the weather to decide if I can fit in outdoor activities like gym sessions or sailing. If the weather isn't suitable, I'll plan indoor activities like co-op games or a workout in my apartment's fitness center. Reading is the easiest to fit in – I make time for it before bed. It's a great way to unwind after a long day. By planning ahead, I can ensure that I have time for all the things I enjoy.
store.17: I enjoy combining my hobbies to create unique experiences. For example, I've spent a day sailing in the morning, followed by lunch, and then spent the evening playing video games with friends. It was fascinating to see how the experience on the water was similar to coordinating movement in an online co-op. Both require teamwork, attention to detail, and problem-solving. I love how each hobby demands these skills in different ways. It's great to have a variety of activities that challenge me and keep me engaged.
store.18: I believe that when you're passionate about your hobbies, you'll always find ways to make time for them, even if it's just in small increments. Whether it's reading one chapter, sailing once a month, or playing a quick match, every bit counts. It's about being intentional with the time you have and finding ways to fit in the things that bring you joy. By doing so, you can maintain a healthy balance between your academic responsibilities and your hobbies. Keep finding ways to make time for the things you love!
store.19: I'm glad you have a diverse range of hobbies that bring different aspects of yourself to the table. It's great to have something unique to talk about outside of coding, and it adds variety to your life. From the calming experience of reading to the thrill of sailing, the discipline of weightlifting to the excitement of co-op games, each hobby contributes to your overall enjoyment. It's wonderful that you appreciate the value of these activities in making your life interesting. Keep exploring and expressing your passions!
